hints: Compare the bonding environment of Cl in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ with that in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$, thinking about what the Cl lone pair can interact with in each case.
Think about how overlap of a Cl p-orbital with the benzene pi system would change the C-Cl bond order and the energy needed to break it in nucleophilic substitution by $\text{OH}^-$.
walkthrough:
Picture the two C-Cl bonds**
In chloroethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{-Cl}$, the C-Cl bond is a simple single sigma bond. The Cl sits on a saturated $sp^3$ carbon with no pi system nearby. In chlorobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-Cl}$, the Cl is attached directly to an $sp^2$ carbon that is part of the delocalised benzene ring.

See the lone pair delocalisation**
Chlorine has three lone pairs in p-orbitals. In chlorobenzene one of these p-orbitals can sit side on to the benzene pi system and overlap with it. That lets electron density from Cl delocalise into the ring. You can draw this as a resonance form with $\text{C}=\text{Cl}^+$ double bond character.

Link to reactivity with hydroxide**
Nucleophilic substitution by $\text{OH}^-$ needs the C-Cl bond to break. Because of that overlap, the C-Cl bond in chlorobenzene is shorter and stronger than a normal single bond, it has partial double bond character. It needs much more energy to break, so chlorobenzene is essentially unreactive to aqueous $\text{OH}^-$ under conditions where chloroethane hydrolyses readily.

Final answer: Chloroethane is more reactive than chlorobenzene toward $\text{OH}^-(aq)$.
The lone pair / p-orbital on Cl overlaps and delocalises into the benzene pi system, giving the C-Cl bond partial double bond character / strengthening it, so it is harder to break.

hints: Identify the parent acid chain including the carbonyl carbon and count from the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ carbon as C1 to locate the Cl and the ethyl ester group.
walkthrough:
Name T like an ester**
T is $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The acyl part has 3 carbons including the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ carbon, so it is a propanoate. The alkoxy part is ethoxy from ethanol, so ethyl. Number from the carbonyl C as C1, then Cl is on C3. That gives ethyl 3-chloropropanoate.

hints: For T with excess hot $\text{NaOH}(aq)$, remember both the ester group and the alkyl chloride can react, what sodium salt and what small alcohol form?
For the nitrile ester with excess hot $\text{HCl}(aq)$, recall that both $\text{-COOR}$ and $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ hydrolyse fully to carboxylic acid groups under acidic heat.

Track the carbon skeleton from $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOR}$ through $\text{NCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOR}$ to Z, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}\text{NO}_2$, what functional group change keeps the ester intact but changes N?
Use the molecular formula of Z to check that the nitrile carbon is retained and the $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ has gained four H atoms to become $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.
walkthrough:
Work out W and X from alkaline hydrolysis**
T has two electrophilic sites: the ester $\text{-COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and the primary alkyl chloride $\text{-CH}_2\text{Cl}$. Hot excess $\text{NaOH}(aq)$ hydrolyses both. The ester gives carboxylate $\text{-COO}^-\text{Na}^+$ plus ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, which is X. The $\text{-CH}_2\text{Cl}$ undergoes substitution by $\text{OH}^-$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$. So W is $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-ONa}$.

Work out Y from double acid hydrolysis**
The starting material for Y is $\text{NC-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-OCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Hot excess $\text{HCl}(aq)$ hydrolyses esters to carboxylic acid plus alcohol, here ethanol is already shown as the co-product. It also hydrolyses nitriles completely: $\text{R-C}\equiv\text{N} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{R-COOH} + \text{NH}_4^+$. So both ends become $\text{-COOH}$. Y is $\text{HO-C(=O)-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-OH}$, butanedioic acid.

Work out Z by reduction**
Step 2 converts $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ to a primary amine while leaving the ester untouched. The formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}\text{NO}_2$ fits addition of 4 H across the nitrile: $\text{NC-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOR} + 4[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOR}$. So Z is $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Final answer: W: $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$ ($\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COONa}$)
X: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$
Y: $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ (butanedioic acid)
Z: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (ethyl 4-aminobutanoate)

hints: Recall how to replace $\text{-Cl}$ by $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ to add one carbon, think of the classic nucleophile and alcoholic solvent for halogenoalkanes.
Recall the two standard ways to convert $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ while keeping an ester group in mind, catalytic hydrogenation or strong hydride.
walkthrough:
Extend the chain with cyanide**
Step 1 is $\text{R-Cl} \rightarrow \text{R-C}\equiv\text{N}$. This is nucleophilic substitution by $\text{CN}^-$. Use $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ dissolved in ethanol, with heat. Ethanol is needed because the halogenoalkane does not dissolve well in water and you want substitution rather than hydrolysis.

Reduce the nitrile to the amine**
Step 2 is $\text{R-C}\equiv\text{N} \rightarrow \text{R-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. This is reduction by hydrogenation: $\text{H}_2$ with Ni or Pt catalyst. $\text{LiAlH}_4$ in dry ether followed by acid work up also works. This adds four H atoms across the triple bond without touching the carbon skeleton.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{KCN}$ / $\text{NaCN}$ in ethanol, heat
step 2: $\text{H}_2$ with Ni / Pt catalyst (heat) OR $\text{LiAlH}_4$

hints: Compare the atoms in $\text{CHCl}_3$ and $\text{CDCl}_3$ and ask which nucleus the proton NMR spectrometer actually detects.
walkthrough:
Why deuterate the solvent**
Proton NMR detects $^1\text{H}$ nuclei only. $\text{CHCl}_3$ has one $^1\text{H}$ and would give a huge absorption that swamps the small sample signals. In $\text{CDCl}_3$, H is replaced by D ($^2\text{H}$), which resonates at a completely different frequency, so the solvent is effectively invisible in the $^1\text{H}$ spectrum.
Final answer: $\text{CDCl}_3$ contains no $^1\text{H}$ so gives no signal / peak in the proton NMR spectrum, whereas $\text{CHCl}_3$ would give a large solvent peak that could obscure sample peaks.

hints: Start with the most shielded peak at $\delta$ 1.2, use Table 8.1 to match it to a plain alkane $\text{CH}_3$ and predict its splitting from the neighbouring $\text{CH}_2$.
Use the $\delta$ 2.2 to 3.0 range to spot the $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C}=\text{O}$ and think about how many protons sit on the adjacent carbon.

For the two downfield peaks at $\delta$ 3.7 and 3.9, both are $\text{CH}_2$ next to an electronegative atom, decide which is next to Cl and which is next to O by comparing electronegativity and the rest of the structure $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
Apply the n+1 rule to each $\text{CH}_2$ to get triplet or quartet, and count protons from the structure to fill the integration column, checking the total is 9 H.
walkthrough:
Assign delta 1.2**
$\delta$ 1.2 falls in 0.9 to 1.7, alkane. In T this is the ester methyl $\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. It sits next to a $\text{CH}_2$ with 2 protons, so n+1 = 3, a triplet. Integration is 3 H.

Assign delta 2.8**
$\delta$ 2.8 falls in 2.2 to 3.0, alkyl next to $\text{C}=\text{O}$. This is $\text{-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-}$, the middle $\text{CH}_2$ next to the carbonyl. Its neighbour is $\text{ClCH}_2$ with 2 protons, so triplet. Integration is 2 H.

Assign delta 3.7**
$\delta$ 3.7 falls in 3.2 to 4.0, alkyl next to electronegative atom. This is $\text{Cl-CH}_2\text{-}$. Cl is less electronegative than O so it appears slightly upfield of the O-$\text{CH}_2$. Neighbour is the $\text{CH}_2\text{C}=\text{O}$ with 2 protons, so triplet. Integration is 2 H.

Assign delta 3.9**
$\delta$ 3.9 is also alkyl next to electronegative atom, but more deshielded because O is more electronegative than Cl. This is $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$. Neighbour is $\text{CH}_3$ with 3 protons, so n+1 = 4, a quartet. Integration is 2 H. The four assignments sum to $3+2+2+2 = 9$ H, matching $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{O}_2\text{Cl}$.

Final answer: $\delta$ 1.2: alkyl / $\text{R-CH}_3$, triplet, 3 H
$\delta$ 2.8: alkyl next to $\text{C}=\text{O}$ / $\text{CH}_2\text{C}=\text{O}$, triplet, 2 H
$\delta$ 3.7: alkyl next to electronegative atom / $\text{CH}_2\text{-Cl}$, triplet, 2 H
$\delta$ 3.9: alkyl next to electronegative atom / $\text{CH}_2\text{-O}$, quartet, 2 H

hints: Look at the group responsible for the $\delta$ 3.9 quartet, $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$, and count how many protons are on the directly attached neighbouring carbon.
walkthrough:
Apply n+1 to the O-CH2**
The $\delta$ 3.9 signal comes from $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$. Its only neighbours are the three equivalent protons of the adjacent $\text{CH}_3$ group. By the n+1 rule, $n = 3$ gives $3+1 = 4$ lines, a quartet.
Final answer: quartet because there are three H atoms on the adjacent / neighbouring C ($\text{CH}_3$), n+1 = 4
